title: 04. Caching: Cache Eviction
summary: Cache eviction is the policy that decides which entries to remove when the cache is full and a new entry must be admitted — common policies include LRU (least recently used), LFU (least frequently used), FIFO, Random, ARC…
objectives: What is cache eviction, and why is the policy choice important?
Compare LRU and LFU. When does each win?
What is scan pollution, and how does it affect LRU?
What is W-TinyLFU, and why does Caffeine use it?

sections.title: Explanation
sections.body:
> **In one line:** Cache eviction is the **policy that decides which entries to remove when the cache is full and a new entry must be admitted** — common policies include LRU (least recently used), LFU (least frequently used), FIFO, Random, ARC (Adaptive Replacement Cache), and W-TinyLFU, each with different hit-rate characteristics on different access patterns.

Every bounded cache must evict — there is always more data than fits in memory, and the cache's value comes from holding the *right* subset. The eviction policy is the algorithm that decides which entries to discard when capacity is exhausted, and the choice of policy can swing hit rate from 30% to 95% on the same workload. The wrong policy fills the cache with cold data and evicts hot data; the right policy keeps the working set resident and absorbs the long tail of one-time accesses without displacing the hot keys. Real-world: Redis exposes `maxmemory-policy` with options including `noeviction` (return errors when full), `allkeys-lru`, `allkeys-lfu`, `allkeys-random`, `volatile-lru` (LRU among keys with TTL), `volatile-lfu`, `volatile-ttl` (evict keys with shortest TTL first), and `volatile-random`; the choice depends on whether the workload is scan-heavy, hot-key-heavy, or mixed. Caffeine (the Java caching library used by Netflix, Uber, and many others) defaults to **W-TinyLFU**, a modern policy that combines admission control (TinyLFU) with a windowed LRU main space, achieving hit rates within 1% of the theoretical maximum on most workloads.

The **fundamental trade-off** is recency vs frequency. **LRU** evicts the entry that was accessed least recently — it assumes "if you haven't used it lately, you won't use it soon." LRU adapts quickly to access pattern shifts (a key that was hot yesterday but cold today gets evicted within a few cache-misses), but it suffers from **scan resistance weakness**: a long sequential scan (e.g., a backup job reading every key once) pollutes the cache, evicting the hot working set, because each scanned key is "more recently used" than the previous hot keys. **LFU** evicts the entry with the lowest access count — it assumes "if you've used it many times, you'll use it again." LFU is scan-resistant (a one-time scan doesn't accumulate enough count to evict high-frequency keys), but it adapts slowly to shifts (a key that was hot yesterday but cold today keeps its high count for a long time, occupying space that should go to new hot keys). Real-world: Redis `allkeys-lru` is appropriate for general workloads; `allkeys-lfu` is appropriate for workloads with stable hot keys and occasional scans (e.g., product catalog with periodic crawls).

**FIFO** (First In First Out) evicts the oldest admitted entry regardless of access pattern — it's the simplest policy (just a queue) but ignores access frequency entirely. FIFO is rarely the best choice, but it's used in write-through caches where every entry is written exactly once and the write order is meaningful (e.g., a write-ahead log buffer). **Random** eviction removes a random entry — surprisingly, Random has competitive hit rates on uniformly-accessed workloads and is trivial to implement in a concurrent setting (no global LRU list to update under lock). Random is used in some Memcached deployments as a low-overhead alternative to LRU. **ARC** (Adaptive Replacement Cache) dynamically balances recency and frequency by maintaining two lists (recently used, frequently used) and adjusting the boundary between them based on hit rates — if recent evictions from the recency list would have been hits in the frequency list, ARC enlarges the frequency list, and vice versa. ARC is self-tuning but complex to implement; it's used in some ZFS deployments and IBM DB2.

**W-TinyLFU** (Caffeine's default) is the modern state of the art. It maintains three spaces: a small **window LRU** (1% of capacity) that admits all new entries to capture recency, a **probationary segment** (80% of capacity) where new admissions are queued, and a **protected segment** (20% of capacity) for entries accessed multiple times. The admission to the main space is governed by **TinyLFU**, which compares the frequency of the candidate entry against the frequency of the victim entry; the candidate is admitted only if it has higher frequency (otherwise it's rejected, and the victim stays). The frequency estimator uses a **Count-Min Sketch** (a probabilistic data structure with sub-byte counters and aging), so memory overhead is small and old frequencies decay over time, allowing adaptation to access pattern shifts. W-TinyLFU achieves hit rates within 1% of the optimal (Belady's MIN) on the Zipf-distributed workloads typical of web caches, which is why Caffeine, Hazelcast, and other modern caches adopt it. Real-world: Netflix uses Caffeine (W-TinyLFU) for in-process caching; Redis 4.0+ added an LFU mode inspired by similar ideas.

The **workload dictates the policy**. A **Zipf-distributed workload** (where a small number of keys receive most accesses — typical of web pages, product views, user profiles) benefits from LFU or W-TinyLFU because the hot keys are stable and frequency is a strong predictor. A **temporal-locality workload** (where the most recently accessed keys are likely to be re-accessed soon — typical of session data, recently-viewed lists) benefits from LRU. A **scan-heavy workload** (where the cache periodically sees a long sequential read of cold keys — typical of batch jobs, backups, crawls) requires scan resistance, so LFU or W-TinyLFU is essential; LRU would be demolished. A **uniformly-distributed workload** (where all keys are equally likely — rare in practice but seen in some hash-partitioned systems) doesn't benefit much from any policy; Random or FIFO is fine. Real-world: Amazon's product page cache uses LFU-like policies (hot products are stable); Netflix's session cache uses LRU (recently-watched predicts next-watch).

The **hit-rate impact** is dramatic. On a Zipf workload with 80/20 distribution (20% of keys get 80% of accesses) and a cache sized at 10% of the working set, LRU achieves ~75% hit rate, LFU achieves ~80%, and W-TinyLFU achieves ~82%. On a scan-heavy workload (90% Zipf, 10% sequential scan), LRU drops to ~55% hit rate (scan pollutes the cache), while LFU and W-TinyLFU hold at ~78% — a 23-point swing that translates directly to database load. On a uniformly-random workload, all policies converge to ~10% (the cache size as a fraction of the working set) — no policy helps, and the cache is essentially random. The lesson: there is no universally-best eviction policy; the right choice depends on the access pattern, and measuring hit rate on the production workload is the only way to be sure.

The **implementation cost** varies. LRU is O(1) per access via hashmap + doubly-linked list (move accessed node to head; evict tail). LFU is O(log n) per access via a min-heap or frequency bucket structure. W-TinyLFU is O(1) amortized per access via the Count-Min Sketch. ARC is O(1) per access but the bookkeeping is complex. FIFO and Random are O(1) and trivial. In a high-throughput cache (millions of ops/sec), the lock contention on the global LRU list can be a bottleneck; modern implementations use **segmented LRU** (multiple LRU lists, one per shard, each with its own lock) or **lock-free** approaches (Caffeine uses a non-blocking design with the sketch as the bottleneck). Real-world: Redis uses an approximate LRU (samples N keys and evicts the least recently used among the sample) to avoid maintaining a global linked list — `maxmemory-samples` defaults to 5; the approximation is within a few percent of true LRU at much lower CPU cost.

sections.body:
### Mermaid Diagram
```mermaid
flowchart TD
    Full[Cache is FULL] --> New[New key request: miss]
    New --> Policy{Eviction Policy?}
    Policy -->|LRU| LRU1[Find least-recently-used entry]
    Policy -->|LFU| LFU1[Find lowest access count]
    Policy -->|FIFO| FIFO1[Find oldest admitted entry]
    Policy -->|Random| Rand1[Pick random entry]
    Policy -->|ARC| ARC1[Adaptive: balance recency vs frequency]
    Policy -->|W-TinyLFU| WTL1[Compare candidate freq vs victim freq via Count-Min Sketch]

    LRU1 --> Evict[Evict victim, admit new]
    LFU1 --> Evict
    FIFO1 --> Evict
    Rand1 --> Evict
    ARC1 --> Evict
    WTL1 --> Admit{Candidate freq > victim freq?}
    Admit -->|Yes| Evict
    Admit -->|No| Reject[Reject candidate, keep victim]
```

### ASCII Diagram
```
Cache full, new key arrives -> pick eviction policy

LRU:       evict entry accessed longest ago
+---+---+---+---+---+
| A | B | C | D | E |   access order:  A (oldest) -> E (newest)
+---+---+---+---+---+   evict A (least recently used)

LFU:       evict entry with lowest access count
+---+---+---+---+---+
| A | B | C | D | E |
| 2 | 5 | 1 | 8 | 3 |   access counts
+---+---+---+---+---+   evict C (count=1, lowest)

FIFO:      evict entry admitted first (queue order)
+---+---+---+---+---+
| A | B | C | D | E |   admission order: A (first) -> E (last)
+---+---+---+---+---+   evict A (oldest in queue, regardless of access)

Random:    evict a random entry
+---+---+---+---+---+
| A | B | C | D | E |   pick any (e.g., random.randint(0,4))
+---+---+---+---+---+   evict random one

W-TinyLFU: admit new only if its estimated frequency
           exceeds the victim's frequency (via Count-Min Sketch)
+---+---+---+---+---+
| A | B | C | D | E |
| 2 | 5 | 1 | 8 | 3 |   victim=C (count=1)
+---+---+---+---+---+
new key F has estimated freq=4  -> 4 > 1  -> admit F, evict C
new key G has estimated freq=0  -> 0 < 1  -> reject G, keep C
```

### Walkthrough
1. **Cache full**: A request arrives for a key not in the cache, but the cache is at capacity — an existing entry must be evicted to make room. The eviction policy is invoked to choose the victim.
2. **Policy decides**: LRU picks the entry accessed longest ago (the tail of the recency list). LFU picks the entry with the lowest access count. FIFO picks the entry admitted earliest. Random picks any. W-TinyLFU compares the candidate's frequency (from the Count-Min Sketch) against the victim's frequency and admits only if higher — otherwise the candidate is rejected and the victim stays.
3. **Admit new**: The victim is removed (its memory is freed), the new entry is inserted, and the metadata (recency list, frequency count, admission timestamp) is updated. The choice of policy determines whether the cache converges on the hot working set or gets polluted by cold scans.

sections.title: Code
sections.body:
**What this code covers**

- Generate a Zipf-distributed sequence of key accesses.
- LRU via OrderedDict.
- LFU via frequency dict.
- FIFO via deque.
- Compare eviction policies (LRU, LFU, FIFO, Random) on a Zipf-distributed
- Workload. Reports hit rate for each policy.
- Workload generator: Zipf-distributed key access
- Precompute CDF for Zipf distribution over keys 1..num_keys.

**Defines:** `zipf_workload()`, `LRUPolicy`, `LFUPolicy`, `FIFOPolicy`, `RandomPolicy`

```python
# Compare eviction policies (LRU, LFU, FIFO, Random) on a Zipf-distributed
# workload. Reports hit rate for each policy.

import random
import heapq
from collections import OrderedDict, defaultdict, deque
from typing import Any

# ---------- Workload generator: Zipf-distributed key access ---------- #
def zipf_workload(num_keys: int, num_requests: int, s: float = 1.0) -> list:
    """Generate a Zipf-distributed sequence of key accesses.

    A small number of keys receive most accesses (typical of web workloads).
    s=1.0 gives a strong skew; s=0 gives uniform.
    """
    # Precompute CDF for Zipf distribution over keys 1..num_keys.
    harmonic = sum(1.0 / (i ** s) for i in range(1, num_keys + 1))
    cdf = []
    cumulative = 0.0
    for i in range(1, num_keys + 1):
        cumulative += (1.0 / (i ** s)) / harmonic
        cdf.append(cumulative)
    requests = []
    for _ in range(num_requests):
        r = random.random()
        # Binary search for the smallest key whose CDF >= r.
        lo, hi = 0, num_keys - 1
        while lo < hi:
            mid = (lo + hi) // 2
            if cdf[mid] < r:
                lo = mid + 1
            else:
                hi = mid
        requests.append(lo + 1)  # keys are 1-indexed
    return requests

# ---------- Eviction policies ---------- #
class LRUPolicy:
    """LRU via OrderedDict. O(1) get/put."""
    def __init__(self, capacity: int):
        self.cap = capacity
        self.store: OrderedDict = OrderedDict()
        self.hits = 0
        self.misses = 0

    def access(self, key: Any) -> None:
        if key in self.store:
            self.store.move_to_end(key)  # mark as recently used
            self.hits += 1
        else:
            self.misses += 1
            if len(self.store) >= self.cap:
                self.store.popitem(last=False)  # evict oldest (FIFO end)
            self.store[key] = True

class LFUPolicy:
    """LFU via frequency dict. Evicts lowest-count entry (ties: LRU)."""
    def __init__(self, capacity: int):
        self.cap = capacity
        self.counts: dict = defaultdict(int)
        self.last_used: dict = {}
        self.clock = 0
        self.hits = 0
        self.misses = 0

    def access(self, key: Any) -> None:
        self.clock += 1
        if self.counts[key] > 0:
            self.hits += 1
        else:
            self.misses += 1
            if len([k for k, v in self.counts.items() if v > 0]) >= self.cap:
                # Find lowest-count entry (tie-break by oldest last_used).
                resident = [k for k, v in self.counts.items() if v > 0]
                victim = min(resident,
                             key=lambda k: (self.counts[k], self.last_used[k]))
                self.counts[victim] = 0  # evict
        self.counts[key] += 1
        self.last_used[key] = self.clock

class FIFOPolicy:
    """FIFO via deque. Evicts oldest admitted."""
    def __init__(self, capacity: int):
        self.cap = capacity
        self.queue = deque()
        self.present = set()
        self.hits = 0
        self.misses = 0

    def access(self, key: Any) -> None:
        if key in self.present:
            self.hits += 1
        else:
            self.misses += 1
            if len(self.queue) >= self.cap:
                victim = self.queue.popleft()
                self.present.discard(victim)
            self.queue.append(key)
            self.present.add(key)

class RandomPolicy:
    """Random eviction."""
    def __init__(self, capacity: int):
        self.cap = capacity
        self.items = []
        self.present = set()
        self.hits = 0
        self.misses = 0

    def access(self, key: Any) -> None:
        if key in self.present:
            self.hits += 1
        else:
            self.misses += 1
            if len(self.items) >= self.cap:
                idx = random.randrange(len(self.items))
                victim = self.items[idx]
                self.items[idx] = key  # replace in place
                self.present.discard(victim)
                self.present.add(key)
            else:
                self.items.append(key)
                self.present.add(key)

# ---------- Run comparison ---------- #
if __name__ == "__main__":
    NUM_KEYS = 1000
    NUM_REQUESTS = 100_000
    CACHE_CAP = 100  # 10% of working set

    print(f"Workload: {NUM_REQUESTS} requests over {NUM_KEYS} keys, "
          f"Zipf(s=1.0), cache capacity={CACHE_CAP} (10% of keys)")
    print()

    requests = zipf_workload(NUM_KEYS, NUM_REQUESTS, s=1.0)

    policies = {
        "LRU    ": LRUPolicy(CACHE_CAP),
        "LFU    ": LFUPolicy(CACHE_CAP),
        "FIFO   ": FIFOPolicy(CACHE_CAP),
        "Random ": RandomPolicy(CACHE_CAP),
    }

    for name, p in policies.items():
        for key in requests:
            p.access(key)
        hit_rate = p.hits / (p.hits + p.misses) * 100
        print(f"  {name}: hit_rate={hit_rate:.1f}%  "
              f"(hits={p.hits}, misses={p.misses})")

    print()
    print("Typical result: LFU >= LRU > FIFO ~= Random on Zipf workload.")
    print("On scan-heavy workloads, LRU drops sharply; LFU holds (scan-resistant).")
```

quiz.explanation: Cache eviction is the algorithm that decides which entries to remove when the cache is full and a new entry must be admitted. Every bounded cache must evict (memory is finite, working sets are larger than caches), and the eviction policy is what determines whether the cache holds the "right" entries — the ones that will be re-accessed — or fills with cold data.
